data.title: El Sayed: I'll go through metal detector if Trump sits for lie detector
data.description:
Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Thursday responded to President Trump’s suggestion that the Democratic candidate should be forced to go through a metal detector at the U.S. Capitol if elected to Congress.

During a campaign rally in Kalamazoo, Mich., El-Sayed said he would accept the request if Trump agreed to “sit for a lie detector.” 

He referenced the president’s ties to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Trump’s unsubstantiated claims that he won the 2020 presidential election. 

“I’ll go through a metal detector every day. You sit through a lie detector one time,” El-Sayed said. “That’s the deal.”  

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis pushed back on El-Sayed’s accusation about Trump’s ties to Epstein in a statement shared with The Hill on Friday afternoon.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein,” Bis wrote. “And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

El-Sayed is engaged in a tight race against Trump-backed GOP nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.).

The president and Rogers have repeatedly attacked the Democratic nominee for his faith and background and accused him of having ties to Islamic extremist groups. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if he wins Michigan’s open Senate race, has denied these accusations. 

During his Thursday rally, the Democrat also used the president’s repeated calls for voters to vote like he was “on the ballot” this November against him. 

“Kalamazoo, on Tuesday, I want you to vote like Donald Trump is on the ballot because Donald Trump is on the ballot,” El-Sayed told the crowd. “His war in Iran is on the ballot. His tariff war is on the ballot. His big ugly bill is on the ballot.”

As of a Friday forecast, nonpartisan election handicapper Decision Desk HQ places El-Sayed’s chances of winning the November race at a 73 percent probability and Rogers’s odds at around a 27 percent probability. The Cook Political Report rates this race as a “toss up.”

The winner of this contest will replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. 

El-Sayed narrowly clinched the nomination over the summer in his primary against Rep. Haley Stevens (D). The lawmaker is expected to rally with the progressive candidate over the weekend, even after her fiancé said he would support Rogers.

data.title: Vance on Trump talking about GOP senator's 'a—': 'I'm jealous'
data.description:
Vice President Vance joked Thursday he is “jealous” President Trump has repeatedly praised other male politicians’ appearances, namely that of Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), and not his own.

Asked by Fox News’ Jesse Watters during a town hall why the president continues to compliment Husted’s backside, Vance laughed it off, saying Trump is a comedian.

“Well, first of all, I’m jealous. The president’s never said that about me,” Vance said. “Get back in the gym maybe and draw that particular piece of praise.”

Throughout his October campaign rally blitz, Trump has shouted out several GOP lawmakers’ and candidates’ physiques, including Sens. Tim Sheehy (Mont.) and Bill Hagerty (Tenn.). But none have received as much attention as Husted.

“I made the mistake of saying that I started off by studying his a—,” Trump said at a Tuesday rally in Texas.

“His a— is like, it’s like a pile of muscle,” the president said in North Carolina on TKTK.

The Washington Post even joined into the bit, creating a quiz for readers about which men Trump has called attractive. The test highlights that not all Trump endorsees had received such compliments from the president surrounding their looks.

For example, during his midterm convention in Dallas, Trump said state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, “may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.”

During the Fox interview, Watters floated the topic of the Texas Senate candidate’s rear end to Vance, to which the vice president responded, “I’m sure Paxton’s doing great.”

Vance said Trump’s playful compliments are one of his favorite things about the president.

“The president, as you know, is at heart a comedian, and he loves to get up there and shake things up a little bit,” Vance said. “I just think it’s a good example of a politician who doesn’t take himself so seriously.”

The vice president, in the final stretch of the midterm campaign, used the moment to focus on Husted as a candidate, calling the Ohio Republican’s opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), a “lunatic.”

“Jon Husted, in addition to his very nice body, is more importantly going to make a much better senator for the people of the United States of America than the lunatic he’s running against,” Vance said.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Brown a 55 percent chance to win the Ohio Senate race.

data.title: Navy airman recounts USS Lincoln leap: 'If I was supposed to die then I would have just been dead'
data.description:
One of the eight sailors who attempted suicide by jumping overboard during the grueling deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier strike group is speaking out after he was effectively punished for the incident.  

Navy airman Nicholas McKelvey, 19, jumped overboard on Aug. 3, 255 days into the ship’s deployment, The New York Times reported.

McKelvey, an aviation mechanic in a helicopter squadron, told the outlet he had been working 12-hour shifts on the flight deck in extreme heat with limited food, had missed the birth of his daughter and was dealing with in-laws battling cancer when he hit his limit and jumped into the Arabian Sea.

U.S. Navy records reviewed by the Times said he was rescued by a helicopter crew and returned to the ship 50 minutes later, with a report on the incident seeming skeptical of what caused him to take the leap.

In the report, an officer acknowledged that it had been “a difficult deployment” and that “it is unsurprising that we might have a jumper.” But they also said McKelvey’s “motives are undetermined” and “the conditions in which he jumped appear suspect,” pointing to the fact he wore his “float coat,” a vest that can be used as a flotation device.

“I didn’t want to be there anymore,” the airman told the Times. “If I was going to die because of it, then that’s just how it is.”

He later added: “Obviously, I was trying to get home. I kept my float coat on because if I wasn’t supposed to die then I was going to get saved, but it didn’t matter, and if I was supposed to die then I would have just been dead. It’s that simple.”

The Navy on Thursday moved to discharge McKelvey, accusing him of faking a mental health crisis to end his deployment, making him ineligible for education assistance under the GI Bill of Rights.

The Lincoln earlier this month docked in San Diego, completing its 322-day deployment, which was expected to end this summer but was extended as part of the war against Iran. The aircraft carrier had helped enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the region. 

The deployment has come under intense scrutiny due to the tight food supplies and degrading mental health on board the massive ship and its strike group. The Lincoln did not have a port call for 286 days until it finally docked in Thailand for a short period last month.  

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao later revealed there had been eight suicide attempts during the lengthy deployment. 

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has conceded the Lincoln’s crew members operated in a tough environment but accused the news media of attempting to “turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission.” 

But McKelvey and his wife, Samantha Larry, said they are speaking out now because they believe he received inadequate mental health care before and after his jump, making his punishment unfair.

The sailor said in June that he visited the ship’s medical unit for mental health care but was directed to speak with a chaplain, a choice he declined, according to the Times. 

The Lincoln only had six mental health specialists for a ship of more than 5,000 service members.

“They don’t want to take accountability for what happened to him, and to what happened to multiple sailors on the boat,” Larry said about her husband. “I don’t think that they care.”

She added, “They care more about how they’re pictured, how they’re viewed. They don’t want anyone to see the bad stuff.”

The Navy charged McKelvey with malingering and “absence without leave” for abandoning his post when he jumped, according to the charging papers, reviewed by the outlet.

data.title: Comey lawyers fight for dismissal of third criminal prosecution
data.description:
Lawyers for James Comey tried to persuade a federal judge on Friday that the Trump administration’s third attempt to prosecute the former FBI Director for allegedly disclosing national defense information should be stopped because the Justice Department (DOJ) waited too long to bring the charges.  

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden, an appointee of President Trump, is weighing whether the criminal case against Comey should be thrown out. He did not rule from the bench.  

One of Comey’s attorneys, Ephraim McDowell, told the judge during a hearing at the federal courthouse in D.C. that the case was “time barred and must be dismissed.”  

“The government has had 10 years,” McDowell said, arguing that the DOJ waited until the “last minute” to pursue the charges.  

Comey is facing two espionage-related charges in connection with the alleged leak of sensitive national defense information to the media a decade ago. Comey has denied any wrongdoing.  

“Nothing’s changed with me,” he said in a Monday afternoon video posted to his Substack account. “I’m still innocent but I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent judiciary.”   

He was not present in the courtroom; however, it was the first time proceedings in the case were held in the open as it had been under seal since Monday.  

The DOJ alleges that Comey directed an individual within this office on Oct. 5, 2016, to share classified information with a The New York Times reporter to correct information that had earlier appeared in a separate Reuters article.  

Comey is seeking to dismiss the case, arguing it is invalid because prosecutors did not secure an indictment before the 10-year statute of limitations ran out. McDowell asserted that federal law was “unambiguous” about that requirement.  

“I think you should hold the government to the words Congress wrote,” he said.  

His lawyers also noted that the disclosure had been investigated by two separate U.S. attorney’s offices previously, both of whom declined to bring charges. 

The new charges were brought by criminal information, which is filed only by a prosecutor and does not require the input of a grand jury.  

DOJ attorney Dustin Farahnak acknowledged that the government used that method to “toll the statute of limitations” while it continues to present evidence to a grand jury. He urged McFadden not to rule on Comey’s request until that process was played out.  

“We had a clock problem,” Farahnak said.  

McFadden also questioned if Comey’s dismissal motion was premature, asking McDowell what the “harm” would be waiting to see what the grand jury does.  

“Aren’t we getting a little ahead of ourselves?” the judge asked.  

McDowell argued the prosecution shouldn’t be “hanging over Mr. Comey’s head,” noting that FBI agents had been stationed outside his home. 

When the judge warned that he would be “extremely frustrated if there’s some kind of dawn raid,” Farahnak assured that was “not going to happen.” 

The DOJ has faced setbacks as it tries to pursue politically sensitive cases in Trump’s second term, with grand juries showing more reluctance. A federal grand jury on Monday declined to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchnison in connection with congressional testimony she gave related to the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, according to reports.  

“Ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days,” McFadden joked during the hearing, referencing an old adage.  

It is the third time since the start of Trump’s second term that the Justice Department has pursued criminal charges against Comey, a move critics see as part of a pressure campaign from the president to investigate his perceived political enemies.  

An attempt to prosecute him last year for allegedly lying in 2020 congressional testimony fell apart after a federal judge found that the prosecutor who secured the indictment, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed as the interim U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia. 

Comey is also pushing to have a case against him in North Carolina tossed, arguing the charges brought by the DOJ over a since-deleted social media post of seashells arranged to read “86 47″ are vindictive.  

Trump and his allies widely interpreted the post to be a deliberate threat against the 47th president, but Comey has maintained that he did not know the numbers could be associated with violence.

data.title: Live updates: Judge orders investigation into DOJ and East Potomac Park; Trump set to rally in Daytona Beach
data.description:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has opened an investigation into the Justice Department (DOJ)’s conduct in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump’s desire to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links.

She ordered the probe during Friday’s hearing, the latest fiery courtroom clash.

Meanwhile, lawyers for James Comey tried to persuade a federal judge on Friday that the Trump administration’s third attempt to prosecute the former FBI director for allegedly disclosing national defense information should be stopped because DOJ waited too long to bring charges.  

Trump is kicking off his final weekend of campaigning ahead of the midterms in the Sunshine State on Friday, after scratching and then rescheduling rallies in Kansas and Iowa planned for this weekend.

Trump is set to speak in Daytona Beach, Fla., around 7 p.m. to vouch for Sen. Ashley Moody (R) in her race against state Rep. Angie Nixon (D) and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds (R) in his highly contested battle against Democrat David Jolly.

Following some mixed messaging, the president will visit Kanas and Iowa this weekend after all. He initially planned to hold a rally in the Sunflower State, supporting incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) against pastor Adam Hamilton (D) in a surprisingly close Senate contest, on Saturday. But, he’ll now hold rallies in both Kansas and Iowa, where both the gubernatorial and Senate races are close in the usually-red Hawkeye State, on Sunday.

The president will also hold tele-rallies this weekend in Texas, New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Montana and South Carolina.

Follow live below.

data.title: Judge opens East Potomac Park probe into potential DOJ misconduct
data.description:
A federal judge has opened an investigation into concerns that the Trump administration lied to her in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump’s desire to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links.

Friday’s hearing became the latest fiery courtroom clash between U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes and the Justice Department (DOJ), which repeatedly took issue with the judge’s lines of questioning and pushed back on any suggestion that information was wrongly withheld.

“The court will open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and DOJ attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules,” the judge said.

A preservationist group and local golfers are suing to stop major redevelopments at East Potomac Park, the longtime home of a public golf course along the edge of the nation’s capital. Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire to redevelop it into a championship-style course, and in recent days, he has said the site will close beginning Nov. 15 so the project can proceed.

The president’s comments — and recent work to cut down hundreds of trees — have escalated the legal fight.

In a flurry of recent hearings in Reyes’s courtroom, the Biden-appointed judge has repeatedly torn into DOJ attorneys about their representations on the status of the project, suggesting they were telling her something different and to not believe the president.

Reyes began on Friday by reminding the DOJ’s No. 3 official, Stanley Woodward, about professional ethics rules he is bound to follow as an attorney practicing before the court. As they continued to spar, the judge at one point told Woodward to “finish that thought internally” and to “talk about it at drinks with your friends.”

“We’re not on TV. I’m not a pundit,” Woodward pushed back at another point, also suggesting some of the judge’s questioning was blocked under executive privilege.

The judge announced she was opening the investigation after learning that the government has been working to submit the redesign plan to the National Capital Planning Commission, which examines major government projects in the Washington, D.C., area. Reyes expressed frustration that DOJ hadn’t previously told her about it. She said she’ll conduct the investigation herself or appoint a special master to do so.

As of now, the judge has restricted further tree-clearing at the golf course and has implemented new notice requirements, but she hasn’t yet outright blocked the planned closure.

“Trust but verify….no longer,” Reyes warned the government.

data.title: Education Department posts doctored image showing its HQ as Spirit Halloween
data.description:
The Education Department on Friday posted a doctored image on X showing the agency’s headquarters in Washington, D.C., with a “Spirit Halloween” banner on the building.

“These things are just popping up everywhere!” the department said in its post.

The image, posted the day before Halloween, comes as President Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon work toward a goal of closing the agency entirely.

The Education Department has made over a dozen deals with other federal agencies to outsource its responsibilities, such as moving the student loan portfolio to the Treasury Department. It has also fired thousands of employees. 

The post was faced with pushback from opponents who believe the recent moves will have a negative effect on schools and students.  

“I get asked by reporters all of the time, “Why don’t student loan borrowers trust the guidence from the federal government in repaying their loans?” Daniel Collier, an expert in higher education, posted on BlueSky. 

“From now on, I am just going to email them this post,” he added, referring to the Education Department’s image 

The Nevada State Education Association said that the department “used to play a critical role in ensuring that students with specific needs were protected, fed, and adequately supported. The dismantling, supported by Trump, McMahon, and [GOP Gov. Joe] Lombardo, will hurt Nevadans.” 

The Hill has reached out to the Education Department for comment.

data.title: ICE agent indicted in Texas after striking immigrant with vehicle
data.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who hit and injured a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas, was indicted by a grand jury in Harris County on Friday.

The 33-year-old officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was indicted on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly driving his vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez earlier this month, NBC News reported.

“The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said in a news conference on Friday, according to NBC.

“An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone,” Teare said.

Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old immigrant without legal status, was driving to work when federal authorities attempted to pull him over. He stopped his car, and he and his passenger attempted to run away.

Surveillance footage from the incident shows the two men running away while an SUV veers and hits Parra Hernandez, who suffered multiple injuries to his leg.

An ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to NBC that the indictment “is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians.” The spokesperson said that only federal agencies can investigate “federal officers acting in the course of their duties.”

At the press conference, Teare said that is “false.”

Following the incident, ICE said that officers observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. An immigration advocacy group, FIEL Houston, said the alleged suspect died years ago based on documentation provided by the man’s family, The New York Times reported.

In an earlier statement to The Hill, an ICE spokesperson said the claims that a federal officer purposefully hit Parra Hernandez are “RECKLESS and FALSE.”

data.title: Meta settles with second plaintiff during trial over social media addiction
data.description:
Meta settled a social media addiction lawsuit with an 18-year-old plaintiff on Friday, avoiding its next bellweather trial, which began jury selection this week.

The case, filed by a woman from Mississippi dubbed “K.D.B.,” alleged her use of Instagram and Snapchat as a child worsened her mental health and contributed to her eating disorder, suicidal thoughts, depression and self-harm.

K.D.B.’s case against Meta and Snap was consolidated with another plaintiff named S.J.’s claims against the company. Their legal teams argue the platforms intentionally designed their platforms to be addictive to young users.

In settling the case, Meta will avoid sitting through another high-profile trial during which CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, were expected to testify. Both Zuckerberg and Mosseri testified in previous trials over similar claims.

The trial will still move forward next week against Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, the plaintiffs’ attorneys confirmed.

Like K.D.B., S..J. is a teenager from Illinois who said she started using Snapchat at a young age, accessing features like “Snapstreaks” and “Snapscore” along with filters and push notifications.

Her suit alleges the features played a role in her compulsive use of Snapchat and contributed to her depression, eating disorder, anxiety and harm.

S.J. also settled her claims with Meta last week.

Emily Jeffcott, a Morgan & Morgan attorney representing K.D.B., said in a statement Friday the team remains “committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client.”

A spokesperson for Meta said “trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellweather process, and this litigation is no exception.”

Jury selection began this week and continued Friday. Jury selection is expected to continue Monday and Tuesday, followed by opening arguments the next day. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify, which will mark his first trial testimony.

Snap did not comment on the settlement news Friday.

Ahead of the trial’s start earlier this week,  a Snapchat spokesperson said the company was “built differently” from traditional social media platforms, arguing the claims “fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences” on the platform. 

Snapchat “opens to a camera, not a feed, not a ranking of what other people post or other social comparison metrics,” the spokesperson said. “We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first.” 

In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement for similar claims, ending a high-profile trial that was already underway in California. The settlement involved 47 U.S. states, three territories and the District of Columbia after Meta said it approached “nearly every state” to collaborate on a safety framework.  

Meta also agreed to pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations.

Along with the payments, the company also agreed to set default daily time limits of two hours for users younger than 18 that can only be lifted by a parent, and it introduced blocks during the nighttime and blocked notifications during school hours. 

Meta’s spokesperson touted this agreement in a statement Friday.

“We’ve spent more than a decade building protections for teens,” the spokesperson said, adding “We hope the rest of our industry joins us in setting this new standard.”
